topics.title: THC, CBD and the cannabis plant
topics.summary: Cannabis contains cannabinoids, terpenes and flavonoids. Delta-9 THC is its main intoxicating cannabinoid; CBD does not produce the characteristic THC high, but still has biological effects. Cannabinoids are concentrated in female flowers. Hemp seed oil is a food oil with little or no cannabinoids and is different from CBD extract.
topics.voice: THC is the main intoxicating cannabinoid; CBD lacks its characteristic high but is biologically active. Female flowers concentrate cannabinoids. Hemp seed oil is not CBD extract.

topics.title: The endocannabinoid system
topics.evidence: Established biology; effects depend on context
topics.summary: The body has a cannabinoid signaling system. CB1 receptors are prominent in nervous tissue; CB2 is associated with immune tissues. THC interacts with these receptors. A biological mechanism alone does not demonstrate a clinical treatment benefit.
topics.voice: CB1: nervous system; CB2: immune tissues. Mechanism does not prove clinical benefit.

topics.title: CBG, CBN, CBC and THCV
topics.summary: Cannabigerol (CBG), cannabinol (CBN), cannabichromene (CBC) and tetrahydrocannabivarin (THCV) are distinct cannabinoids under investigation. Research interest does not establish a treatment, a safe personal dose, or a reliable effect from a retail label. Do not turn laboratory findings into promises that CBN treats insomnia or THCV produces weight loss.
topics.voice: CBG, CBN, CBC and THCV are research topics, not established retail treatments. Do not promise CBN sleep benefits or THCV weight loss.

topics.title: Terpenes and the entourage hypothesis
topics.evidence: Chemistry established; clinical claims remain limited
topics.summary: Terpenes contribute to cannabis aroma. Common research targets include myrcene, limonene, pinene and beta-caryophyllene. The entourage hypothesis proposes interactions among plant compounds; it is not a guarantee of a particular therapeutic effect. A controlled 2024 human study found limonene reduced some THC-related anxiety under specific experimental conditions. That does not establish that a limonene-rich strain treats anxiety.
topics.voice: Terpenes contribute aroma. Entourage effects are hypotheses, not guaranteed treatments. A controlled limonene/THC study does not prove a named strain treats anxiety.

topics.title: Why a strain name is not a medical profile
topics.summary: Names and indica/sativa/hybrid labels do not reliably establish chemical composition or medicinal effects. The same name can vary between producers and batches. This library is not a complete strain registry. For an unverified name, MaryJain says so instead of inventing lineage, potency, terpenes or therapeutic benefits.
topics.voice: No complete strain registry is loaded. Names and indica/sativa/hybrid labels cannot guarantee chemistry or effects. Never invent lineage, potency or medicinal benefits for an unfamiliar name.

topics.title: Chemotypes, genetics and batch variation
topics.summary: Common chemical groupings are THC-dominant, mixed THC/CBD and CBD-dominant. Genetics, growing conditions and preparation can affect measured composition even with clones. A chemotype describes chemistry, not an approved medical indication.
topics.voice: Chemotypes describe THC-dominant, mixed or CBD-dominant chemistry. Genetics, growing conditions and preparation can change batch composition, even with clones.

topics.title: What research actually says about named examples
topics.evidence: One chemical dataset; not clinical trials
topics.summary: In a 2022 commercial-flower dataset, Blue Dream often clustered with myrcene/pinene, Dutch Treat with terpinolene, and Purple Punch and Dogwalker OG with caryophyllene/limonene. Tangie was less chemically consistent. These are observations within that dataset, not guaranteed batch profiles or evidence of medicinal effects.
topics.voice: 2022 chemistry dataset: Blue Dream—myrcene/pinene; Dutch Treat—terpinolene; Purple Punch/Dogwalker OG—caryophyllene/limonene; Tangie less consistent. Dataset tendencies only, never batch guarantees or medical claims.

topics.title: Approved cannabinoid medicines
topics.summary: In the United States, prescription cannabidiol (Epidiolex) has specific seizure indications: Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex in patients aged one year and older. Dronabinol and nabilone have specific chemotherapy-related nausea indications; dronabinol also has an AIDS-related anorexia/weight-loss indication. These approvals concern defined medicines and populations, not dispensary strains or retail CBD generally.
topics.voice: FDA approvals: Epidiolex for seizures in Lennox–Gastaut, Dravet and tuberous sclerosis complex, age 1+; dronabinol/nabilone for specified chemotherapy nausea; dronabinol for AIDS-related anorexia/weight loss. Retail strains are not equivalent.

topics.title: Chronic pain: modest effects and meaningful gaps
topics.evidence: 2025 systematic review; low to moderate certainty
topics.summary: AHRQ’s 2025 review found small short-term pain improvements, largely in neuropathic pain studies, with certain THC-containing formulations. Dizziness, sedation and nausea increased. Oral CBD alone did not improve pain in the included trials. Evidence for whole-plant cannabis, long-term outcomes and reducing opioid use remained insufficient. These results do not rank retail strains or establish a personal treatment plan.
topics.voice: AHRQ 2025: certain THC formulations gave small short-term pain benefits with more dizziness, sedation and nausea. Oral CBD alone did not improve pain; whole-plant and long-term evidence remained insufficient.

topics.title: Cancer symptoms are different from cancer treatment
topics.evidence: Specific symptom indications; no proven cancer cure
topics.summary: Some cannabinoid medicines can treat chemotherapy-related nausea when conventional antiemetics have been inadequate. That is different from treating the cancer itself. Laboratory antitumor findings do not establish a cure in people, and cannabis is not an FDA-approved cancer treatment. Cancer patients should discuss cannabis and possible treatment interactions with their oncology team.
topics.voice: Chemotherapy nausea relief is not cancer treatment. Laboratory antitumor findings do not prove a human cure. Do not suggest replacing oncology treatment.

topics.title: Multiple sclerosis and spasticity
topics.summary: Some cannabinoid preparations have modest evidence for patient-reported multiple-sclerosis spasticity symptoms. Objective measures have been less consistent. Symptom improvement does not establish disease modification, and findings from a studied preparation do not apply automatically to a named strain.
topics.voice: Some preparations modestly improve reported MS spasticity; objective findings are less consistent. This is symptom research, not a cure or strain-specific evidence.

topics.title: Sleep, bowel disease and glaucoma claims
topics.summary: Sleep improvements in studies of other illnesses may reflect symptom relief rather than a direct insomnia treatment. Evidence for primary sleep problems is uncertain. Symptom changes in bowel-disease studies do not prove remission. Cannabis is not an established glaucoma treatment. An individual’s care decisions require a qualified clinician.
topics.voice: Primary insomnia evidence is uncertain. Bowel symptom relief is not proven remission. Cannabis is not an established glaucoma treatment.

topics.title: Anxiety, paranoia and psychosis
topics.evidence: Risks observed; causation and susceptibility vary
topics.summary: Cannabis can cause anxiety, paranoia and disorientation. Use is associated with psychosis and schizophrenia, especially with earlier initiation and more frequent use, but individual risk cannot be predicted from a strain label. A feeling of short-term relaxation is not proof that cannabis treats an anxiety disorder or depression.
topics.voice: Cannabis can cause anxiety/paranoia; frequent and earlier use is linked with psychosis risk. Relaxation anecdotes are not established anxiety or depression treatments.

topics.title: PTSD and trauma-related claims
topics.summary: The VA/DoD’s 2023 PTSD guideline recommends against treating PTSD with cannabis or cannabis derivatives. Research has not established an effective PTSD treatment, despite anecdotal reports of relief. MaryJain can explain that evidence distinction and encourage evidence-based care without dismissing a person’s experience.
topics.voice: VA/DoD 2023 recommends against cannabis as PTSD treatment. Anecdotal relief does not establish efficacy; acknowledge experiences without presenting them as clinical proof.

topics.title: CBD, medicines and liver effects
topics.summary: CBD can affect the action of other medicines and can cause liver injury and sedation. Combining it with alcohol or sedating medicines can increase drowsiness. Non-intoxicating does not mean risk-free. A pharmacist or prescribing clinician should assess an individual’s medicines; the assistant cannot clear a combination or tell someone to stop a prescription.
topics.voice: CBD can cause liver injury, sedation and drug interactions. A pharmacist/clinician must assess personal combinations. Never tell a visitor to stop or change prescriptions.

topics.title: Does CBD cancel THC?
topics.summary: CBD is not a reliable antidote to THC. A controlled oral-administration study found stronger effects and impairment with a high-CBD/THC combination than with THC alone. Route, amount and timing matter; this result should not be generalized to every preparation or used as a home-treatment protocol.
topics.voice: CBD does not reliably cancel THC. A controlled oral study found greater effects and impairment with high CBD plus THC. Do not offer CBD as an antidote.

topics.title: Edibles, delayed effects and accidental exposure
topics.summary: Edibles may take 30 minutes to two hours to produce intoxicating effects, and effects can last longer than expected. Delayed onset increases accidental overconsumption risk. Keep cannabis locked away from children and pets. Suspected poisoning warrants prompt poison-center guidance; in the US call 1-800-222-1222, or 911 for an emergency. Do not use a timing estimate as a redosing instruction.
topics.voice: Edibles can have delayed, prolonged effects; no redosing advice. Lock away from children/pets. Suspected poisoning: US Poison Control 1-800-222-1222; emergency 911, or local equivalents.

topics.title: Concentrates, tolerance and cannabis use disorder
topics.evidence: Established risk; precise individual risk varies
topics.summary: Concentrates can contain much more THC than flower. Higher THC is not a guarantee of better medical benefit. Cannabis use disorder can involve loss of control and continued use despite harm; risk increases with earlier initiation and frequent use. Increasing tolerance does not mean someone is immune to impairment. Support from a health professional can help when use is becoming difficult to control.
topics.voice: Concentrates can deliver high THC; potency is not medical quality. Frequent/earlier use raises dependence risk. Tolerance does not remove impairment; support is available.

topics.title: Delta-8 and novel cannabinoid products
topics.summary: Delta-8 THC is intoxicating. FDA reports concerns about unapproved products, variable composition and contaminants from conversion processes. A hemp-derived label does not establish safety or legal status. This library does not establish clinical benefits or reliable potency equivalence for delta-10, HHC or THCP products.
topics.voice: Delta-8 is intoxicating; FDA notes variable products and conversion-contaminant concerns. Hemp-derived is not a safety guarantee. Novel cannabinoid benefits/equivalencies are not established here.

topics.title: Driving, work and impairment
topics.summary: Cannabis can impair reaction time, coordination and judgment. Alcohol and cannabis together can increase impairment. A measured THC level or feeling normal cannot reliably certify fitness to drive. MaryJain does not provide a personalized safe-to-drive countdown; choose transportation with a sober driver when impairment is possible.
topics.voice: Cannabis impairs driving skills; alcohol can worsen impairment. No THC-level shortcut or guaranteed safe-to-drive countdown. Use a sober driver.

topics.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
topics.summary: Cannabis exposure during pregnancy may affect fetal development, and chemicals from cannabis can pass into breast milk. CBD is not established as a safe substitute. CDC encourages avoiding cannabis while breastfeeding and discussing use with a clinician during pregnancy, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
topics.voice: Pregnancy/breastfeeding: no safe cannabis or CBD substitute is established; discuss with a clinician. Cannabis chemicals can reach a baby through breast milk.

topics.title: Lung and cardiovascular effects
topics.evidence: Known effects plus observational risk evidence
topics.summary: Cannabis smoke contains irritants and can harm lung tissue; smoking is associated with cough and bronchitis symptoms. Cannabis can acutely increase heart rate and blood pressure. Associations with cardiovascular events require careful interpretation because smoke exposure and other factors can confound findings. No inhaled product should be presented as risk-free.
topics.voice: Smoke harms lungs and can cause bronchitis symptoms. Cannabis can raise heart rate/blood pressure; cardiovascular associations have confounders. Do not call inhaled products risk-free.

topics.title: Cannabinoid hyperemesis
topics.summary: Some long-term cannabis users develop recurrent severe vomiting, known as cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome. Vomiting should not automatically be attributed to cannabis; medical assessment is needed, especially with dehydration or severe symptoms. MaryJain cannot diagnose the cause or offer a home-treatment protocol.
topics.voice: Repeated severe vomiting can occur with long-term use (CHS), but do not diagnose it. Severe symptoms or dehydration need medical assessment.

topics.title: Reading a certificate of analysis
topics.summary: A certificate of analysis (COA) reports test results for a particular sample or batch. California testing includes cannabinoids, terpenes, pesticides, residual solvents, heavy metals, microbes, mycotoxins and other quality measures. Match the report to the batch and distinguish a test result from a medical claim. A passed panel does not prove a treatment works or eliminate every possible risk.
topics.voice: COAs report batch tests, not medical efficacy. Match batch identity; distinguish cannabinoids/terpenes from contaminant panels. California requirements are examples, not universal law.

topics.title: Potency numbers and measurement quality
topics.summary: Laboratories need consistent methods and reference materials to produce comparable cannabinoid measurements. Acidic and neutral cannabinoid measurements are not interchangeable. Compare units, sample identity, method and reporting limits before comparing numbers. A printed percentage cannot verify a batch’s identity, predict a person’s experience or establish therapeutic quality.
topics.voice: Potency interpretation requires units, sample identity, method and reporting limits. Acidic/neutral cannabinoids differ; a percentage does not predict personal effects or medicinal quality.

topics.title: How the industry fits together
topics.summary: Cultivation, manufacturing, testing, distribution and retail are distinct activities in California’s licensing system; delivery is part of its retail framework. Rules vary by jurisdiction and change. This library is not a current legal, tax or licensing opinion. An AI can explain terminology and routine policies, while authorized staff handle regulated decisions and transactions.
topics.voice: Explain cultivation/manufacturing/testing/distribution/retail roles. California is only an example. No live law/tax/license verification; authorized staff handle regulated decisions and transactions.
